utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We'll start with an administrative hearing in which Dr. Falke will respond to any remaining questions. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, is it your intention to do this in open session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was my next line, whether the Defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I know that the line often has been that there's nothing to be hidden and therefore we could deal with matters in open session, but I want to verify again whether that is also true for the present situation. It is. Then we'll remain in open session. Yes, but before we ask Dr. Falke to come in, I would like to deal with one matter about health reports. At the end of yesterday's session, the Registry was invited to provide the Prosecution with any additional information related to the health of the accused which it had not yet received. The latest report by the RMO which was filed before the parties just yesterday is dated the 29th of May, 2013. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to file any such future reports on the record until further notice, subject - I would say of course - to the accused's consent. Having dealt with that, could Dr. Falke be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Falke, please be seated. Good morning to you. Could you put on your earphones. Yes. We asked the -- to receive -- to obtain further information about the recent reports, various reports, about the health of Mr. Mladic and the recommendations made therein. Dr. Falke, could I first ask you, have you read the report of the 29th of May, that is, the last report?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yes, I did. All reports are written and discussed by -- with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then perhaps before we start, for those who are not familiar with your position, could you please explain in one or two lines what your position is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yes, sure, Your Honour. I'm the medical officer at the United Nations Detention Unit for the last 15 years. My main role is being the treating physician for the accused, detained persons, for the ICTY. And in that role, I am end responsible for the given health care to these detained persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We usually receive the reports, as you know, from the medical officer. We have a few questions, focusing primarily on what has changed since the arrival of Mr. Mladic; and second, what has changed since the April report in which you come with new recommendations -- well, at least the reporting medical officer comes with new recommendations to reduce the sitting schedule to four days a week. First, during the first period of time, apart from periods of ill health, such as pneumonia, I remember there was a small surgical intervention once, but apart from these incidental matters, what has from a medical point of view changed since the arrival of Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Maybe I take the risk to talk as a physician, as a medical physician, to judicial trained people and often there is a different level of understanding. So I try to be as clear as possible. In medicine we differentiate evidence-based and experience-based medicine, and I think it's important to understand that not everything in health care and in medicine can be proven by diagnostic tests as black and white as it sounds. Often diagnoses are made by observations, discussions between physicians and other care-takers, and that is more of an experience-based level. As you may aware of, taking in account the earlier reports, Mr. Mladic is known to have had two strokes in the past and is a man of an age of 71 years old. That is, those are objective findings. Also, earlier CT scans made of the brain show some damage due to these strokes, so there is a permanent change and damage. Nevertheless, recent CT scan did not show further abnormalities. So there seems to be a stable situation. Recent performed neuropsychological assessment did not show explicit or major lesion in the cognition or other cerebral dysfunction. Cardiac assessment did show a reasonable good condition of his heart, taking into account his age. And his blood pressure, which is mentioned quite often, though fluctuating under stress, recuperates well to normal levels in rest periods. He did develop somewhat of diabetes over time with us and he experienced some weight loss, be it discreet there is some weight loss. And earlier performed imaging shows general arthrosclerosis of the neck and cerebral arteries and some peripheral arteries as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any change in that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: No, no. There is no change in that. And maybe I could come back to that later, but that's partly due to the close monitoring since he arrived at the UNDU and the treatment he gets. The reason -- what we noticed, not only me but also members of my medical team, although less objective findings but observations by clinical experienced people, sometimes based on validated assessments, assessment tests, nevertheless, is a discreet increase of his residual symptoms after the strokes, like an increase of slower and slurred speech, reduced muscle strength, especially after a working day --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just ask, Doctor, is that something that is normal after a stroke for anybody?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yes, partly. Yeah. And most of the people who experience a stroke, therefore, do not work or do not work any more because often experience fatigue which happens much quicker in people who experience strokes show more of the residual symptoms, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one question. You said observations by clinical experienced people. Who do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Sorry, I should have explained the team members. The treatment team consists of three groups. There is the group at the medical service, so the MO and my deputy; the nurses and the RMOs on certain distance; there is the psycho medical overview team that means on a weekly basis most of the time, and that includes next to them teams of the medical service, a psychiatrist. And there is the team of the clinical physicians, mainly at Bronovo Hospital that consist of a neurologist, a cardiologist, a gerontologist, radiologist, urologist, and a neuropsychologist. And they all helped me to assess the present situation of Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me then. You are giving us the composition of the team. My question was clinical experienced people. Now who do you mean by those? Would that include the urologist, for example?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yes, although he has not a major input in the questions involved here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the radiologist?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah, it's the same, but he's part of the team of all the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But my question was you rely on, as you said, clinical experienced people and their observations, so therefore I would like to know which ones do play a role and which ones do not play a role.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: When it comes to explaining the performed diagnostic tests, of course, also radiology is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the second. You said sometimes supported by. I'll come to that in my next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah. But mainly, mainly -- well, myself and my deputy medical officer being general practitioners and judicial physicians for a long time. The psychiatrist involved, it's a Dutch psychiatrist who works for the NIFP, Dutch forensic psychiatric service, and also the RMOs, one of the RMO is in a very experienced occupational and forensic physician and the other is an experienced general practitioner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so you say it's mainly you, the forensics -- the psychiatrist and the reporting medical officer, that is the core. Could you tell us for how long in a week -- how often would you see Mr. Mladic for how long?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: It differs from week to week, but I'm in on Monday afternoon and Wednesday and Friday, and most of the time I see him for a short or a longer period during that week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And all together how many minutes? Half-hours? Quarters of an hour would that be on average in a week?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: On average, I would say between 30 minutes and one and one half hours, something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: And that's just me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's just you, yes. You explained about these observations. You said they were supported by clinical tests. Could you further elaborate on the clinical tests?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yes, the neurologist performed another CT scan of the brain. The cardiologist made a CT scan of the transformation to see if the coronary arteries -- in what condition they were in. The gerontologist and the neuropsychologist, they performed a neuropsychological assessment. I think those are the main assessments performed by the clinical physicians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the reduced muscle strength was measured and -- I do understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By whom and what was the result?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah, I mentioned a discreet increase in residual symptoms, like reduction of muscle strength.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: And it is -- it was assessed by both myself as well as the physiotherapist as well as the reporting medical officer, the gerontologist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I'm a bit confused. You say that it was -- the observations were based on validated assessments, assessment tests which show the discreet increase of the residual symptoms. Compared to what? If you're talking about muscle strength, compared to when and how measured at the time you compared with?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Mladic is in the United Nations Detention Unit since 2011.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: And so over this -- during this -- this period up till now he is seen by these people just mentioned more often, and gradually there has been a change. The major change assessed by these people were found in the beginning -- at the end of last year and the beginning of this year. In the team there is a discussion going on in relation to the reduction of -- an advice for a reduction of court schedule for a longer period than since the RMO first mentioned the advice. But of course, you have to go through some time to sustain your suspicion or your observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say it was based on validated assessment and then you said "assessment tests." I -- what I hear now from you is a kind of a general assessment, not specific tests. And I was mainly focusing on the reduced muscle strength. Could you give the details about how that was measured, observed, assessed, and what -- how it was validated?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: When I was referring to validated assessment tests, I was not referring to a muscle strength test. I was coming to that. It was mainly the psychiatric evaluation -- the evaluation of the psychiatrist who uses validated assessment tests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And what was the conclusion of those -- those tests? Now -- we are now talking about validated tests. I do understand that is then limited to psychiatric --

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah. Observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- observations -- well, at least examinations.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah, examinations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was the outcome? What was the conclusion of those tests?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: That -- that there was a reduction of concentration span, that there was an increased fatigue, especially during weekdays where the team concluded that it was difficult to differentiate the cause of these symptoms, whether it was due to his personality structure, his residual symptoms after strokes, or stress -- the normal stress that detention and trial proceedings show to any person. So it was -- the psychiatrist mainly concluded that at least part of these symptoms that increased over the last months were due to the residual symptoms by stroke but also partly -- partly due by his personality structure that causes him and his surroundings on an awful lot of stress.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I -- exactly in relation to what you just told us, I would like to put a question to you. That was my -- when you first spoke about the -- your assessment tests, I was wondering how you can distinguish between those changes resulting from residual symptoms of former strokes or just in relation to age?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How can you distinguish by real medical assessment?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Well, you've got a point there and that's why I also already --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're not here to make points, Mr. Falke. We're just trying to --

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- fully understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah. No, I understand. That is not always easy to distinguish and that's why I already mentioned earlier that it is not often always evidence-based but also experience-based that clinical evaluations and dialogues with other physicians, conclusions can develop. And these conclusions are based on different expertise by different physicians and other care-takers, who sometimes use validated assessment tests, that's their background, like psychiatrists they -- and psychiatric evaluation is based on validated tests, not that a psychiatrist does, strictly speaking, does a test or an examination, a psychiatric examination, every time, but observes and taking in account the knowledge of the tests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To clarify that a little bit more, when you spoke about that first, you said members of my medical team noticed, although less objective findings, but observations by clinical experienced people. This is exactly what you just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But you said sometimes based on validated assessments. I just want -- would like to know, are your -- is your assessment only based on the tests conducted by the psychiatrist or do you have any other more objective medical findings you can base your opinion on?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Well, as I mentioned earlier, that is the problem. Often medicine is not based on evidence, based on hard facts, but based on experience, on observations, and clinical observations. And the clinical observations done by different members of the team are an increased fatigue, are a reduction of concentration span, are a reduction of emotional control, and a decrease of abilities for self care. And these symptoms can be related to different issues, residual symptoms, stress, and personality issues, and physical disabilities. And it's very difficult to get clear what the percentage of the different causes is that -- that is involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You told us about observations since 2011.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is the psychiatrist involved the same today as in 2011?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Almost I think. I'm -- I don't have the exact dates, but she's involved for at least a year now, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were talking about the deterioration more or less observed by the psychiatrist I think you said over the last month, let's say the last five, six months this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has this been jotted down anywhere on paper? I noticed today -- I mean in the daily reporting, would it -- could the Chamber have a -- get an impression of what is written there so that we can see how it was observed and what was noted in that respect? Is there a possibility --

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Well, there are different kind of observations written down. Of course, the guards observe detained person and write down in the log-book if people are asleep or awake during the night, if they are restless, whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They're not specifically trained for that but they --

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: They are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- act on the basis of --

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: No, they are trained for that. They are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, of course you can see whether someone is sleeping or not, but for example, assessments of activity or assessment of stress, et cetera, are they specifically trained for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yes, that's part of their profession. Guards -- guards are not just people who stand in front of a cell door; they are people who are involved in the well being of detained persons. And therefore, they are trained to observe whether things go well or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How are they trained for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: That's not my expertise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but apparently you tell us that they are trained in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then at least in order to rely on their observations --

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you would need to know exactly how they developed expertise in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: No, I don't agree, with all due respect. That's the management who is responsible for the training of the guards and that's not me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but you --

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: -- I rely -- I rely on the management to make sure that the guards are trained and do well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what you're telling us, you suppose that they're sufficiently trained --

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to make those observations, but you have no personal knowledge --

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- on how they were trained and what level of expertise they have developed in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah, that's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Yes, I have one additional question -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just in relation to that, you told us about the observations made by the physiotherapist.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Was that also a general observation or did he conduct any measurement?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Well, he sees the detained person twice a week and he has specific exercises he performs and every day -- every time he sees the patient. So yes, he assesses whether the exercises he performs with the patient have any result or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Was that written in the log-book or in the medical documentation somewhere?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yes, not on a regular basis, I have to admit, but if and when the physiotherapist discusses this with me or one of my team members, it is written down in the medical file, yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have access to any such observations specifically on the physiotherapy and the findings of the physiotherapist?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then my next question is: Since when is Mr. Mladic assisted by a physiotherapist?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: I -- I think almost -- right from the start, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: With the same frequency?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: More or less, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Depending on court schedules and availability of the physiotherapist, but on the average I would say at least once a week and most of the time twice a week, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. A specific question for you is the following: Have you received and read the report which was drafted by experts hired by Defence counsel who pointed at an elevated risk of -- in relation to the blood pressure, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any comments on that report?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us those comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: When I read these reports, they show concern for the patient they examined. That's the first thing. Well, that's good to read. I differ from opinion when it comes to the conclusions. I'm a bit reluctant to say so, nevertheless, whether -- it is -- I can understand also the Chamber asks themselves: Well, what is the increased risk that another incident, cerebral incident, will happen? Because that would have large consequences for the trial proceedings and whatever, also for his own health of course. Peaks in blood pressure, like in Mr. Mladic's case happens especially during stress periods and of course at the moment going to trial are these stress periods, do have -- do not have an increased risk of a stroke as he experienced in the past, that was a non-bleeding stroke, so a thrombosis, it was not a bleeding. Those strokes, non-bleeding strokes, only happen if a blood pressure for a long period is not well under control. It's the same with cardiac incidents, even if people do not have coronary problems, if there's a long high blood pressure stress, continuous stress, it could create a heart incident as well. So it is -- I read the reports and I discussed this with one of the treating neurologists, to be sure whether I was right in my different opinion, and he agreed with that. He -- there is no reason, so far - not seen in the scans or whatever - to be afraid of bleeding in the brain, so bleeding stroke that is not very likely to happen. It is a worst-case scenario, and that's what I think these experts talk about, it's a worst-case scenario, but it is it likely? No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just with respect to the blood pressure, does Mr. Mladic receive medication with the aim to lower his blood pressure?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yes, he does and right from the start when he entered the UNDU his -- he came in in a reasonably bad state. And from then on he was closely monitored by different clinical specialists and the medical service. His medication was brought up to normal levels and it showed -- and also the physiotherapy and it all showed improvement in his health status.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How do you make sure that he is taking the medication?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, one of the advantages of being a doctor in a prison is that you can be sure that there is no non-compliance when it comes to medication because the medication is distributed to the detained person by the guards and they have to take the medication in the presence of the guards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one question in that context. We have had in the past a problem with one of the detainees who after careful examination there was a serious suspicion that in a similar situation he did not take his medication or he spat it out soon after the guards had left. I know that in that case the situation was adapted, but you're so clear now. Does that mean that the guards are staying with Mr. Mladic for half an hour after he takes his medication?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: No, I don't think so and I'm not sure whether you refer to a situation in 2005 and 2006?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yes, that was not a situation, as far as I'm concerned because I was the physician at present at that time, that was not a situation of not taking the medication; it was a situation of taking medication that was not prescribed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it went in stages. The first stage --

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- was, Dr. Falke, that he spat out most likely his medication, and once there was a better control on taking the medication, the effect improved significantly. And it was only after that that the other medication was apparently taken not prescribed. Is my recollection right that the stages of what you described were as I say and not just the second part as you told us?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. What I was trying to refer to is that when it comes to at that time the blood pressure that was not under control and we couldn't get it under control was maybe in the beginning part of the non-compliance. But there was -- the main problem was something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now I have -- Judge Moloto has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Dr. Falke, notwithstanding your difference with the doctors that were employed by Mr. Mladic on their conclusions, is it -- are we to understand that notwithstanding that difference you are still in agreement with their recommendations? Because it looks like the recommendations they make are exactly the same as the recommendations that are made by the UNDU doctors?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yes, maybe on slightly different conclusions, but I still agree with my team and I still believe in the advice we gave for a reduction in the court schedule. And of course both myself and my team fully respect and are aware of the difficulties we create with this advice, and it's not up to us whether the advice is indeed accepted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We understand that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah. But that is nevertheless -- I mean, my responsibility as MO is primarily with the patient and that's what I have to take into account primarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you the following question: If -- unless you have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not done yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, what would be the kind of result that you would have envisaged based on your medical -- your conclusions which differ from those of the doctors that were employed by Mr. Mladic? Because they're talking of something that could actually result into a fatal stroke.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is the result that you are trying to obviate by your recommendations?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What my question is -- well, they're saying if Mr. Mladic -- if we don't reduce the time for sitting, the possibility that he might get a stroke which is -- could be fatal becomes a reality. You're saying that's a worst-case scenario and it's not likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm saying: What then is the unfortunate result, based on your findings, that you want to make sure doesn't eventuate by your recommendations?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. The -- it is I think about what we would call in the medical world tertiary prevention. You see symptoms related, partly related, to a medical condition and to prohibit a more serious outcome you try to do something to reduce --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is the serious outcome? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: The outcome could, for example -- one of the outcomes, and that's what one of the psychiatrists also mentioned, could be a burn-out due to extreme fatigue. So I don't think about strokes at the moment. If -- would the blood pressure stay high, then that would be a realistic complication but that's not the case yet and hopefully it will not be. But it's mainly, it's mainly, the symptoms like a reduction of self care, the reduction of concentration span, the reduction of emotional control, the fatigue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It could worsen those --

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yes, and finally it could come to a complete break-down, to a burn-out, and that is much more realistic. So taking in account his age, all the issues mentioned, he is somewhat more vulnerable, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you the following: An elevated blood pressure in moments of stress, is that a medical abnormality or is that a relatively normal situation to which Mr. Mladic unfortunately is more frequently exposed to than ordinary persons?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, it depends on the height of the blood pressure. In all of us as we sit here in situations of stress, blood pressure will elevate. In exercise, which is also a form of physical stress, it will lower. But -- and that's why exercise is also good for the blood pressure. But in stress, in mental stress, it will rise and that is, in fact, a reasonable normal physiological process because the heart rate increases and therefore the output increases and output is related to part of the blood pressure. The height in Mr. Mladic measured were somewhat abnormal I would say. If a blood pressure is 180 over 100, 110, that is too much. I mean, in normal people it would be between 140, 160. Sistole and diastole, maybe between 90 and 100 max.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also in stress situations?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how often did you measure such?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Well, actually the medical service here measured the blood pressures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but how often was it at such a level that you say that is, as you said, is -- you first were saying somewhat abnormal and then you say 180 over 100 or 110 is too much. How often was -- were these levels measured?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: I'm not exactly know the numbers, but it was exactly -- most of the times the medical service had to come in, there was a period when they had to come in quite often --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, whether they had to come in or whether they were called in --

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Whether they were called in, sorry. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah. They were called. And most of the time the blood pressure was abnormal high.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But my question was: What levels? Are you talking about these levels --

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and how -- that is 180 over 100. And how quickly did it go down again?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Very often he was I think leaving the courtroom and it was measured once again and then it lowered very quickly. Coming back to the UNDU, we left him for an hour and measured it again, it was absolutely normal again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: With the medication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could this reaction to stress be part of the personality structure or is it -- I mean, some people may respond different to stress than others. Is there always a medical explanation or could it also be personality or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Personality structure does a lot with stress. If, for example, you are a narcissistic person and you hear all kind of things -- negative things about yourself in a courtroom, that creates an enormous stress.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you, sorry to do that --

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if we would sit four days a week, would you expect that during the remaining four days, that if there was a stress situation that the high-level blood pressure would be significantly lower --

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- because sitting only four days a week? No, you would say that would be approximately the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: No, because the moment of stress -- the causes are still the same, personality structure, residual symptoms, the normal stress that anybody in such circumstances will experience. So these issues will not be different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And they will not bring the kind of risk as described by the two experts, the risk of a stroke unless you said if it was a more or less continuous remaining high level?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Well, I can't look into the future --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: But from a statistic point of view - and that's what I understood from the neurologist I met last week - a bleeding cerebral vascular accident is a worst-case scenario. Of course it can always happen but it's not likely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As it could happen to everyone at that age?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yes, who would be in such stress situations, of course. If there is a weak vessel in the brain - which of course with general arthrosclerosis like Mr. Mladic - it is possible, but you can't diagnose that where there is a weak wall in a small place but -- so that can also -- but it can happen to anybody here who is not aware of a weak arthrosclerotic vessel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Including you, including counsel, including the Prosecution, and including the Judges, is that more or less --

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Well, the Judges maybe, but doctors never become ill. No, it can happen to all of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Even at different ages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, could I ask you the following. There is a kind of a general cardiological picture. You were talking about statistics. How would be Mr. Mladic's score for the average 71-year-old in terms of cardiological problems, blood pressure? Is that rare? Is that only 1 per cent of the 71-years-old would suffer from it or would it be 15 per cent? I mean, what's the -- if you have an assessment on that on how extraordinary this situation is for a person of his age?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah, well cardiology for that matter is a reasonably simple specialisation because it is reasonably -- well, diagnostics are improved incredibly. One of the main diagnostics when it comes to coronary assessments because coronaries are the main cause of heart infarctions, we can perform a CT scan of the thoracical region and we can measure a calcium score. Calcium, as you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: -- is part of the arthrosclerosis. It is an -- a beautiful measurements and in Mr. Mladic's situation a calcium score performed showed a score of 25 which means for his age is put -- is good. So the risk that he will develop a myocardia-infarction is very small.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: So if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you mentioned too, the CT scan didn't show abnormalities either or -- because you were talking about the CT scan of the thoracical region.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you mentioned the calcium score. You said this calcium score is quite good.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: For his age, it's completely acceptable. That is what you do with the CT scan, you do a calcium score.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so that's normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: If I may add something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: You -- earlier on you were referring to another case and situation in a different time and two -- it's good to mention that not always that cardiac incident is caused by coronary sclerosis. At that time that was an issue as well. Because even with clean coronaries, if you have a blood pressure that is on a high level all the time, at some point you get a stretch of the mucoid, of the muscle of the heart, and it will create a similar situation as an infarction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you explained to us that that is not the situation with Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, you have -- you said you have read the last report. Could I ask you for some of the issues raised therein to find your medical assessment. One of the things mentioned is the loss of weight and you referred to that briefly earlier. First of all, what does it mean in medical terms? When I read here, I see he lost 1 and a half kilos since the last measurement of the unit in April and it -- then it was 76 and it came from 80 kilogrammes in May 2011. What is the message we have to learn from what you write down there, the medical assessment?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah. Reading it again I realise we could have added -- the RMO could have added some extra information there. In itself, losing 6 kilogrammes in one and a half year's time, in two year's time, is not such an issue. But for a person who is reasonably passive, one would expect - with a normal appetite - one would expect an increase of weight, a considerable of weight, especially in his age. He's not a 90-year-old who has an enormous muscle loss, et cetera, et cetera. That's not the case here yet. So in fact, what you look at, it's not a loss of 6 kilogrammes. In fact, it's a higher loss because he should have gained weight. If you eat properly and you do not exercise, your fats and your sugars will be transformed into fats in the body, so you will gain weight. And that's not what happened. And what we noticed in the last few months especially is that he -- his fatigue is increasing. And we, for example, see is that he comes back from court and he even hasn't got the energy to undress himself. He just lies in bed and stays there for a long period and neglects his dinner, his evening meal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could -- is there a possibility that some depressive thoughts could play a role there?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what the team asked themselves as well, and the conclusion is that there are no symptoms of a depression as being psychiatric ailment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now whether it's psychiatric disease or not, I think it's common human experience that you can feel without being diagnosed as with a depression that you sometimes can feel somewhat depressed and have less energy for all kind of things you would under normal circumstances do. So therefore you are saying there is no medical explanation, but in that respect as diagnosed illness. But would you for any medical reason exclude for the possibility that such a reaction, even if not pathological, could be part of the explanation?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Well, experiencing a stressy -- a stressful situation during a day can create emotions, and if emotions are not abnormal in itself even if they are negative, even if they're about anger and sadness and feeling depressed. So yes, in -- for that matter Mr. Mladic is not -- is a normal human being so will react the same way. That's -- although that's not what we observed. What we observed that he was mainly physically very tired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you a few more questions about the weight. You said he lost close to 6 kilogrammes where you would have expected him to gain weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He arrived with a weight of 80 kilogrammes. Could that weight have been caused by certain nutrition habits, eating a lot of fat? I mean, do you know anything about what was the starting situation caused by and whether the circumstances may have considerably changed such as at least healthy food, which -- well, the next thing of course, not being able to consume any alcohol in the detention situation. Have you considered that? Because you expressed some concern about the loss of weight of 6 kilogrammes, whereas if he was neglecting himself by his nutrition habits or by the use of alcohol, I've no idea whether it has been ever established, but is that a possible explanation as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yes, although I doubt it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For what reason?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: If he would have had a bad, unhealthy lifestyle where it comes to food, he should have been much heavier, especially using alcohol, because from alcohol we know there are a lot of sugars, carbon hydrates in there, so these sugars are all transformed into fats in the body. And that's why people using alcohol often especially -- yeah, they often -- they often gain weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, can I ask you an analytical question in this respect. You say I doubt because people who are badly nurtured or are using alcohol should be far heavier. But if you have -- or at least you would expect him to be far heavier than 80 kilogrammes. Now, if there was a moderate unhealthy nutrition scheme and a use of alcohol which was not excessive but at least it was there, I mean how could you possibly make -- well, let's say, if you use alcohol you should have been 85 or 90 kilos?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean, what's the basis for this analysis, apart from what you told us?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: And of course I'm not talking about alcoholism because then these people do not eat anymore and that's why they do not gain weight but lose weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Well, if I look at the food habits in the Detention Unit that I -- my own -- the only conclusion I can draw is that it's not healthy at all. But they cook themselves, they are allowed to buy food. And the bulk of food, although very agreeable and nice, is very rich with a lot of fats, a lot of salt, and a lot of sweets. And that's what they still consume within the Unit. So they hardly eat the prison food offered. They cook themselves most of the time. So for that matter, he is not -- one would -- if he would take the prison food, I would expect a downfall in weight because that is reasonably healthy, reasonably balanced, not very fat, et cetera. But that's not what the detained persons eat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now this is a totally different explanation compared to the previous one. The previous one, he should have been heavier before if he would have bad habits and now you say there are bad habits here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you agree that we don't know all the details of what happened before he arrived -- unless you are measuring how many calories he eats and fats, et cetera, when cooking his own food?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yes, I agree there are maybe too many parameters to be sure what the cause of the weight loss is. I agree completely. But then again, it is a symptom we notice. And like more symptoms, you can't really be sure what the cause is. It's often multi-factual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I understand that you are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- at the moment discussing observations. If you compare the observations in relation to Mr. Mladic with other detainees after their arrival at the Detention Unit, are there any significant difference?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yes, but also due to more factors. A lot of detained persons do sport much more often than they were used to when they were not detained because we have a lot of facilities and they like to go into the fresh air, they like to go do sports. So that's the reason why a lot of detained persons lost weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now could I in relation to this also ask the following. You are comparing -- and that's what you were giving us, 80 kilogrammes arrival, 76 in April, and now -- 74 now, 74, 74 and a half. First of all, is there a routine in the measurement of the weight?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah, it's -- yes, there is. If you mean if it's done regularly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, my primary question would be whether it is always done under similar circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: On the same scale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same scale?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: In the same room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same room. Same time of the day?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: No, not always. Most of the time at the end of the day because he returns from court in the afternoon. So most of the time it's done in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I'm not an expert, but if I go on my own scale on a regular basis, 1 and a half kilogrammes is within the range of a little bit higher today, a little bit less tomorrow. Is -- could you -- is -- from a professional point of view, is a difference of 1 and a half kilogrammes, is that within the normal range of variation?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: No, that would be a lot and that probably would mean that if you -- if it differs 1 and a half kilos, that would mean that you would contain extra fluids like edema in the legs or whatever because 1 and a half kilos is a lot if it differs from one day to another. Of course, you can drink a litre of water and then will gain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: -- you will gain of course. Of course. But that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: -- that's reasonably excessive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, then perhaps I have to see my doctor. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Or your scale maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's -- my next question would be: You're saying he lost weight. Now, if I remember well there was a moment, I think it was approximately one and a half years ago, when Mr. Mladic was suffering from pneumonia and lost much, much, much weight, far below what he is now. And he was then gaining weight again, I think he was under 60 kilogrammes. Now, there's a comparison 80 kilogrammes then perhaps below 60, then 67, that gain of weight that these external circumstances or internal circumstances gives as far as I can see a bit of a different impression. I didn't hear you mentioning it when you explained the numbers I did put to you. Is that a significant matter to consider, that you meanwhile lost 20 kilos or more and then regained weight?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you considered that in expressing your concerns about the loss of 6 kilogrammes?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah. It's like in scientific research you have to take in account a specific period long enough to see the tendency, and of course you can have ups and downs also in -- and measurements also in weight. There can be incidents like pneumonia or another incident where the weight drops. But if you -- that's not what you take into account. You look at the large period where there are stable factors enough to see if the tendency of the measurements are significant or not in the end. And of course when you lose a lot of kilogrammes due to, for example, a pneumonia which is a serious ailment, you have a recuperation time, you will have no court after a recovery from pneumonia, whatever. So you have a lot of possibility to gain weight again to the normal -- I would say the normal level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could you make available to the Chamber the list of weight measurements? And in relation to that I have one additional question. You referred to the last measurement in April. I thought you told us that he was -- his weight was measured on a regular, frequent basis. April is, as far as I'm concerned, four, five, six, seven, eight weeks ago. Is that the frequency with which you measure it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah, that is definitely not on a weekly basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not on a weekly basis?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: No, that -- there again -- there could be fluctuations within a week- or two-week time. Not on a daily base but on a week time, and so it doesn't say anything about the tendency. So you have to take in account -- you have to take dots within the year and of course you can measure it on a daily base, but that is -- doesn't give more information in the end I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it be possible to make available to the Chamber the -- I would say the monthly measurements then or whatever you have on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: I noted, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then my -- in the most recent report attention is paid to the sleeping pattern which is influenced by being woken up. Has there been any change since the last reports and has the necessity of disturbing the sleep of Mr. Mladic be further discussed with the United Nations Detention Unit?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: With the management you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: No. I didn't recently discuss the sleeping pattern with the management.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because it has changed. We understood from the reports it has been reduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then my last question is -- that is partly related to weight. You said that Mr. Mladic finds listening to the evidence of the witness - or witnesses, I take it, in the plural - very painful and disturbing and this also could have added to diminish his appetite. Now, first of all to what extent is that a medical issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Only partly. Any accused listening to witnesses, I charge, would be stressed. Even with a normal -- even without personality issues, even without residual symptoms, if you hear things -- nasty things about yourself, it will cause stress. So that is not a medical -- strictly medical issue, it's a psychological issue, but not a medical -- strictly medical issue. In the situation of Mr. Mladic, there are more causes possible, as just mentioned. So then it can be a medical issue. I say "can be" because we had -- even in the team meetings, it did not became clear what cause had a priority there. Was it the personality structure, abnormalities in the personality structure? Was it the residual symptoms that reduced -- that reduced the emotional control and concentration span? But on the average I would say it would happen to anybody and even more in people with certain personality issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I, just for clarification, ask you the following. You said: "If you hear things, nasty things, about yourself, it will cause stress." In the report itself there is no reference to hearing nasty things about Mr. Mladic himself. Of course the testimony of witnesses, it's not always a pleasure to listen to that, but doesn't that relate to all participants in the court, even to the public gallery?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Oh yes, sure, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: These are not nasty things about the -- the person listening to these events?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: No, it will -- I mean, the things we hear in court here are often awful to all listeners. But being an accused, it is about -- I mean, your -- your actions in the past are at stake or are a part of the discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if that results in a loss of appetite and a loss of weight, then that would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Well, partly, partly physiological, I would say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you don't know which part?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: No. Well, that's a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: That's a problem. And in his situation, we see that it is -- it is going along together with an increasing fatigue, lying in his bed after coming back from court for a long period and not having dinner, that sort of thing. And I can't give you more exact information there, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you ever considered what the medical consequences, if it is predictable at all, would be for an extended trial of six months extra at a -- at an age even higher than Mr. Mladic is in now? And have you considered that in your recommendations?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: I did, but we didn't discuss it in the psycho medical overview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And in your own inner thoughts, what could you share with us, those thoughts?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Well, it is not evidence-based, it is experience-based, having seen a lot of accused in the last 15 years who are all my patients. And some of the trial proceedings were extended quite a bit. Yes, of course, that also has its implications, but it's difficult for me to give any objective or statistic numbers there, what it would mean for the accused or -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say a cost-benefit analysis in this respect you can't make?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: No, I think that's very difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Now, one thing I have to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we decide on how to proceed, have the parties further questions for Dr. Falke? Because if there would be one question which takes two minutes, we might even consider to continue; if there are more questions, then we should take a break first and then -- Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a number of questions and I believe we have been sitting for an hour and 20 minutes at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was -- I should explain to Dr. Falke that we usually stop after one hour following the recommendations as far as pauses are concerned, and I saw that you did not jump up and say that it was irresponsible what we were doing. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We do not have too many questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't have any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe one or two. Two maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But nevertheless, Mr. Groome, it would take you ten minutes or more I take it? If it's a matter of two or three minutes --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it would take more. Then we first take a break. Then we first take a break. I hope that you are still available after a break of 20 minutes, Dr. Falke. We'll then --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just -- I'm not sure that Dr. Falke was informed that we were in public session and I just was wondering whether he is clear that that is how we have been proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps I should have told you but I inquired with the Defence before we started this hearing whether they would prefer to have it in private session. In the past we have experienced that often the Defence had a clear preference for public session. So that's the reason why we moved in public session. But of course also we had in the back of our minds also very much the type of questions we were to put to you. We take a break. Could Dr. Falke be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at 25 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could Dr. Falke be escorted into the courtroom. Please be seated, Dr. Falke. The parties may have some questions for you. Mr. -- perhaps we start with the Defence as the -- any questions at all, Mr. Lukic, or only a few?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Actually, I would like just to make one intervention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I would check it with Dr. Falke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Transcript line 20 -- page 20, line 14, I think it's wrongly recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's check.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says diastole may be 190 maximum --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Probably should be 100 maximum, that's what I heard at that time. I'll read the whole sentence for you so you can -- "If a blood pressure is 180 over 100, 110, that is too much. I mean, in normal people it would be between 140, 160 systole and diastole maybe 190 max." It should be 100, I guess? That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 90 to 100. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- anything else, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only, since we are in a public session and Dr. Falke was explaining us about the possibility of weight loss during the pneumonia, only it wasn't mentioned was at the time when the drastic weight loss occurred with Mr. Mladic that at that time he really had pneumonia?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yes, yeah. There was a relationship definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. That's all I had for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. First, Dr. Falke, I'd like to thank you for coming this morning and helping us understand these issues in greater detail. Now, the medical report we received yesterday is from the 29th of May. Before court started this morning, I was informed that there was some updated information that you wanted to provide orally, and I don't know whether you've done that already or whether you've had an opportunity. So I want to give you an express opportunity now to update us on anything that's happened or any assessments made after this report of the 29th was drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: I have no problem doing that, Your Honour, the only thing is I need the consent of my patient. It can be verbally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could you consult with Mr. Mladic and see whether he agrees that Dr. Falke gives us an update.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, there is consent from Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then also -- of course I've got no idea what the content would be but no need to go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No need, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Dr. Falke.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yes, I -- I was referring to the examinations of the gerontologist that included the neuropsychological assessment previously done. Discussed last week between the gerontologist and the two neuropsychologists involved and last Monday yesterday discussed by the gerontologist with Mr. Mladic the results.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in the 29th of May report, this specific report is referred to and it's indicated that a final report is forthcoming.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Has a final report --

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Not yet, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Can you update us on what the assessment is at this stage with respect to the gerontologist?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah. The neuropsychological assessment is an evidence-based tool to assess cognition damage and cerebral dysfunction in people especially who experienced strokes. The outcome of this neuropsychological assessment as far as I understood from my meeting with the gerontologist yesterday and my telephone conversation with him last Friday, the outcome -- the conclusion is that there are no large cognition damages found nor brain cerebral dysfunctions for that matter. He does have some nuances in his answer because he says we reviewed these neuropsychological -- this psychological assessment with the three of us and what we do see is a decreased concentration span and a decreased emotional control, that could well be related or is likely to be related to the experienced strokes as a sort of -- as a residual -- as residual symptoms. But then again, hundred per cent guarantee there is not possible because it is, as it were, polluted by personality structure issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one additional question in that context. Can it be polluted as well by the circumstances? A decreased emotional control, could that be influenced by what happens in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. Then -- well, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: I can't be a hundred per cent sure. And every time we discussed these outcomes with each other, it was always the trias: with personality issues, residual symptoms, and the actual stress in relation to the situation. So it is, indeed, Your Honour, it's difficult to be absolutely clear. But as far as I understood the gerontologist - but I didn't see it on paper yet but that's what I discussed with him - is that it is very likely that it is a residual symptom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, this assessment which I take from you is being put in a final report, based on your experience is this current assessment of -- this aspect of his health, is that something that you would expect to remain stable or is it something that you would anticipate rapid changes to?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yes, well in fact if there is no new damage to the brains which you can see -- well, at large you can see on a CT scan performed that it's reasonably repeated, if that's not the case then it's not very likely that it will -- that these symptoms will increase in strength and in diversity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the medical report that we received last evening is authored by a Dr. Amanda de Glanville as reporting medical officer. I don't recall seeing her name on a medical report in the past and in fact in most cases we've received them from Dr. Aernout Tenhaeff --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have seen the previous reports by this doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I apologise. I hadn't seen one at all this year, but maybe I missed it but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I remembered. I mean, the name is so familiar to me and doesn't come out of the blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: I have -- let me have a look. I have all the RMO reports here --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It may be unnecessary. All I wanted to establish was whether she had had -- whether she was a new doctor or whether she's had -- is familiar with his care.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Well, see there are two RMOs, two reporting medical officers, Dr. Aernout Tenhaeff and Dr. Amanda de Glanville. And they both write reports on a regular -- on a weekly basis, and there are a few written in relation to Mr. Mladic by Dr. de Glanville and most of them by Aernout Tenhaeff just by coincidence because they have a schedule, a working schedule. And Dr. Tenhaeff is an occupational forensic physician and Dr. de Glanville is a general practitioner.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. I just -- I stand corrected. I wasn't sure how long she had been involved in his care. Now, we know that he's suffered two strokes and has some permanent deficits with respect to speech and strength on the right side of his body. Despite your answers to questions put to you by the Chamber, I'm still not clear about the relationship between the observations in paragraph 3 of the report of the 29th, this loss of strength and his slightly slurred speech, I'm not certain of the relationship between the stroke and the tiredness. Can you please explain that in a little greater detail?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah. Well even if people are very tired without any other ailments, they don't talk with a slurred speech unless they had too much to drink, alcohol, that is. So that is a specific symptom related to residual symptom which sort of increases the moment such a person is fatigued, is tired, because then the control -- the motoric control over the mouth and speech muscles reduces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Judge Moloto put to you and I'm not sure I understood your answer, is that something that we would expect from other stroke victims --

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- with similar deficits that when they become tired you may see this increased difficulty in speech?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yes, especially those muscles that have some neurological input problems will work less in situations of fatigue, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, one of the opinions put forward by the Defence for this application and one that was referred to by the Chamber is the opinion of Dr. Ratko Kvockovic [phoen], and it's dated the 29th November, 2012. In a paragraph in that report, he recounts a discussion he had with Mr. Mladic regarding facts related to this case. The last sentence of that discussion says: "The attempt to confront him with the indictment was discontinued because of the serious risk that the same emotional reaction would be repeated and lead to a transient ischemic attack," or TIA. Do you recall roughly reading that? So my question to you is: Does a transient ischemic attack or a TIA, does that include both types of strokes which you have spoken about today, a bleeding cerebral vascular event as well as a thrombosis.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: No, a TIA is -- it always has to do with a thrombosis because if it would be a bleeding, it would leave permanent damage because you can't take away the bleeding. And the essence of a TIA is that it's only temporary loss of abilities and definitely not more than 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, to your knowledge, is there any scientific medical literature establishing a connection between an emotional reaction and a serious risk or a serious increased risk of a TIA?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: I asked myself this question and so I asked this question to the neurologist, and as far as he could recall there were no clear evidence-based researches done on this particular topic, no. But I didn't -- I have to admit, I didn't have the time to Google meds myself and see what that -- so I'm sorry I have to -- I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, to switch the topic to the interrupted sleep, and paragraph 4 of this report of the 29th of May deals with that, I'm not concerned about the times when he is awoken by nightmares. What I am interested in is do you know how often he is presently being awoken during the night by staff at the UNDU, medical or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah, he's -- yeah, he's on a monitoring regime, as you probably are aware of. And the guards try not to wake up a monitored detained person and sometimes that works and sometimes it doesn't. In Mr. Mladic's situation, I believe he's a light sleeper but he often quickly wakes if he's awake and then he falls asleep again, at least he closes his eyes again. So I can't tell you whether or whether or not he has great sleeping disturbance due to the monitoring. I don't think so because my experience in the past is if people experience disturbance of sleep due to the monitoring regime, they immediately will send a request to the medical service to talk to the doctor to make -- that the doctor makes clear to the management that this is not a good idea and he never did for that matter. But he is on and off awake anyway which in -- partly in age is not abnormal. The older you become the less sleep you need, it's a physiological thing. So that's why old people -- older people more often are awake during the night. And in his situation, he -- I have to admit he never discussed nightmares with me in person. He mentioned that to the reporting medical officer, but in those meetings I'm not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if I can -- can you tell us, give us some idea of how frequently he's monitored, as you put it? Is it every hour, every two hours, three hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: No, his monitoring regime at the moment as far, because we have a lot of people who are monitored, but as far as Mr. Mladic is concerned, I think it's every two hours if I'm right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And for those of us unfamiliar with what --

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Sorry, it's every three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Every three hours. Those of us who are unfamiliar with what is entailed in monitoring, can you just explain briefly what is a monitoring?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: It also depends on the reason why there is a monitor. For example, in Mr. Mladic's situation he experienced strokes in the past and we do not know whether there will be a new stroke in the future. So if a stroke would occur, you would not like to leave a person if it would occur during the night lying in bed for the rest of the night for two reasons. First of all, I think it's inhumane; but secondly, if you react within three hours, you can reverse the symptoms partly due to a new stroke by sending him to a hospital and they have a specific treatment there. So that's why the three hours are there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you said you don't know whether he is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But the question was a little bit different.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Therefore, I would like to repeat that. How does this monitoring --

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- how is it carried out?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: You're right. Excuse me. In his situation, they will open the hatch, that is a blind, iron hatch, in front of the window and the door and see if there is any abnormality seen. There's always a small light in his cell on so they can see the person in bed, but they do not wake him on purpose. There are situations, for example, if someone experienced an incident recently that we -- sorry, sorry. Yeah. If someone experienced an incident recently that we, during the monitoring, we do wake someone up because we want to be absolutely sure that there is no recurrence or no complications of a recent incident. But in his situation, it's just to see if he's restless or awake or if we see -- if the guards see any abnormalities, if he fell out of bed, things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, is it always visible if someone suffered from a stroke -- well, let's say an hour before you look at him, is it -- is there possibility that he seems to be just asleep although he had a stroke?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yes, and that is -- that is often the problem with monitoring, is you have to find a balance between what you try to achieve and disturbing the night rest, which can also cause problems. So sometimes I agree, Your Honour, sometimes we explicitly or the management explicitly orders the staff to wake somebody up. In Mr. Mladic's situation, we have the management whom I advised did not do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, is it a current feature of a stroke that someone starts moving restlessly and that's falling out of bed, for instance?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, it often shows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I think you said that you don't know to your knowledge whether or not the monitoring wakes up Mr. Mladic. Would I be correct in saying that you're not able to exclude the possibility that he is awoken and that this could be a contributing factor to the fatigue he experiences during the day?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: That could be the case, but then often you see that people have a fatigue already waking up in the morning and they mention: I had a bad night or I didn't sleep well or I'm tired because I woke up. That's not the case with Mr. Mladic. As far as I'm concerned, it never -- it didn't show in any log-book of the guards or whatever. So I -- I think that's not the case. It is mainly the fatigue that's built up during the day which is explicitly noticeable on weekdays where he goes to court much more than when he has a day off or weekend day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, it seems that you consider the monitoring medically necessary, so my question is: Are there other alternatives to be able to monitor him during the night, given your concerns, that would have less chance that his sleep is being interrupted?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
