utterances.text: We went through that discussion years ago in -- with other detained persons who were at risk and I remember all kind of discussions about the flaws with sensors and beds with sensors and, well, in the end it was such a complex situation. It also almost became an intensive care unit. So in the end it was -- the conclusion was that the management and I think in the end the Registry also decided not to go that far. And the management of the prison didn't go that way, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So for what --

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: So the monitoring is, in fact, the only thing you have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that also a cost issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it mainly a cost issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Probably, probably, and also I'm not sure whether that's mainly or just a small part, but it is also a reassurance that seems to be very objective and very clear while -- the question is: If someone doesn't fall on the floor, the sensors will not notice anything. If he lies still in bed, those sensors will not do anything. The only thing that would really help - and that's what we used in the past as well - is if the heart would stop beating because you can have a sensor -- a heart rate monitor, that's what we did in the past. But the heart rate will not necessarily change in someone who has a stroke, not necessarily. It can be -- it can be caused by a rhythm disorder, but not necessarily. So it is not only cost, but it will be very costly, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whereas if I understand you well a heart rate monitor is not that expensive?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: No, no, and of course the only thing is -- yeah, a person has to keep it on all night and we know from the past that sometimes it fell off or it -- that happens while turning around in your bed and that wakes up the person as well because then the guards will come and have a look at what's going on and they have to wake him. So it is -- yeah, it has pros and cons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, my next series of questions relates to the recommendation of the medical staff. The Chamber has decided to sit for five days a week during the first three weeks of June. Do you expect or anticipate any medical emergency within the next three weeks as a result of continuing to sit for five days a week?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: I don't expect emergencies as far as I can look into the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: If ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the -- after that period there's about a five-week period before the summer recess. Is it your opinion that working five days a week for that period, up until the summer recess, would negatively impact Mr. Mladic, keeping in mind that he'll have then three weeks to -- with no court hearings?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Well, we already know from the past that it will influence him, he will experience more fatigue, et cetera, et cetera. But if you relate it -- if you would like to relate it to serious incidents, I would say that's not likely going to happen. And if it's only a three-week period there is some horizon to be seen after which there is a break, so that makes a difference. And we noticed in the past because if I look at the court schedule in the last months, last half year, well from the beginning of this year, there has been a lot of weeks with only four or even three days court and we noticed that that definitely made a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That relates to my next question. If the Chamber should grant the application and adopt a four-day-a-week schedule, what would be the objective signs or indicators that that in fact does have a health benefit for him and how long do you think it would take for us to first see such indicators?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: It's a logic question. It's not that easy to answer, I'm afraid. It's also partly -- we have to experience what will happen. What we saw in the past, and that's maybe the best thing for me to answer the question, is looking back into the past, what happened in the past, is that having some break in the week makes it easier for him to recuperate, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, my next set of question concern whether Mr. Mladic currently has any other disease processes that are likely to impact his long-term health? In particular, several weeks ago we were informed that Mr. Mladic suffered some complications as a result of a biopsy. So several weeks ago we were informed that Mr. Mladic suffered some complications as a result of a biopsy exam. My question in this regard is whether a biopsy was performed on Mr. Mladic to investigate whether or not he had some type of cancer and at this stage it's not necessary to identify what particular type of cancer, just whether that's -- is that why a biopsy was done?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah, that's why most of the time biopsies are done. It could also be to make sure whether it's an infection or so, but biopsies are related most of the time to oncology.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you tell us whether the biopsy test was positive or negative for cancer?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: It was negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are there any other health issues which you believe might affect Mr. Mladic's long-term health apart from the ones that you've discussed related to aging?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, maybe his diabetes, and we'll have to see how that will develop in the future. On the other hand, we're on top of it so we -- I intend to treat that as I do with all my diabetes patients. So it's reasonably strict.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, my final questions to you, Doctor, relate to other possible options to ameliorate Mr. Mladic's fatigue. Now, given that a day off in the middle of the week would cause scheduling problems, have you considered whether five shorter days a week would yield similar reductions with respect to reduction of fatigue?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, and actually for me that's very difficult to answer, whether five short days or four longer days with one day in the middle, would make the difference. As medical team we came up with the advice for a day off in the middle of the week, with the idea that that was a moment to recuperate. And I can't give you any evidence whether that would be more beneficial than five shorter court days.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, there is a remote facility in the Detention Unit that would allow Mr. Mladic to participate in the trial remotely. In your opinion, would observing the trial from that room one day a week achieve a similar reduction in fatigue that you hope for in the -- or you anticipate in the four-day court hearing schedule?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Well, it would at least be an interesting pilot to start with. We experienced in the past with one of other accused that it was very helpful at the time, and even if it's only for some period. So I can't say that that wouldn't be an alternative, no definitely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Again, Doctor, I thank you for your time today.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. Mr. Lukic, any further matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't have a question for the doctor, only I would object to the proposal given at the end by the Prosecutor to have Mr. Mladic remotely -- then it would be -- it would further decrease our capability to consult with our client. So I would just kindly ask you not to take that into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we'll ask most likely for submissions by the parties after this hearing. So therefore then you can elaborate on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one last question. You repeatedly were talking about reduced or decreased and it was not always clear to me decreased since when. I just read one part of the transcript. You said: "... this psychological assessment with the three of us and what we do see is a decreased concentration span and a decreased emotional control that could well be related or is likely to be related to the experienced strokes, as is thought of as a residual -- as residual symptoms." Now, when I hear you say "decreased" or sometimes you use "reduced," in this line which I just read to you, do you mean to say that compared to the situation before the stroke it would have been a decreased concentration span and a decreased emotional control, or are you talking about any difference experienced -- so apart from the fatigue but in this respect experienced over the -- well, let's say the last six months?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah. One thing is that several teams -- members of the medical team noticed that in longer conversations where other detained persons would still be concentrated, he lost track of the conversation and what we concluded was that he lost concentration. He was not confused or whatever, but he lost concentration. And he would pick the conversation up again if you would explain to him: Okay, Mr. Mladic, we were talking about this or this or this. Oh, it's okay. And then he would continue. So our experience was that he, especially over the last half year, that he was -- his concentration was reduced. That's one thing. The second thing is that in a neuropsychological assessment done by the Bronovo gerontology team, it also showed a decreased concentration span and that of course is related to -- it is a validated test so it's related to normal groups in that age. It is all relative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My last question: Did you ever include in your findings any -- or I would say include in your analysis any observation of the behaviour of Mr. Mladic in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how did you do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Well, I -- mainly by speaking to the management and I heard what was going on in the courtroom. And I didn't see any images myself of these court sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did they?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did they see them?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah, I think so, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the specialists never have -- well, looked at five or ten hours of performance of Mr. Mladic's behaviour in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions. If there are no -- Mr. Lukic, I was informed that Mr. Mladic would perhaps like to speak a few words at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you know approximately what the limits are of what can be addressed and what --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- cannot be addressed and we'd like to give an opportunity to Mr. Mladic to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He just wants to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to say a few words.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- thank Dr. Falke for his care.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic has an opportunity to express himself if he wishes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask you to tell me how many minutes I have. I would like to address you but in public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, two or three sentences is approximately what may be needed for -- to do it in public. That's where the limits are.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gentlemen, where I am concerned and my health, I would like to have at least five minutes. I'm not Socrates or Pythagoras to say panta rhei: "Everything is in flow, everything changes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If there is any, Mr. Lukic will have an opportunity to make further submissions. Mr. Lukic has had an opportunity to ask any questions he wished from Dr. Falke. Mr. Lukic, we understood that Mr. Mladic would express a few words of thanks. That's what he's allowed to do but not to address the Court or to further elaborate on what we discussed today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gentlemen, Dr. Falke, you, your team, the entire staff in the Detention Unit that is monitoring me, following developments in my case night and day, all the medical staff in the Detention Unit that has been treating me and the medical staff of the Bronovo Hospital, I would like to deeply bow to all of them and greet you all as the people who have pulled me out of a grave by both my legs. Had it not been for your care, for medications, and God's will, I would have visited St. Peter a long time ago. Judges, let me address you and you, Doctor. As a human being, I am not surprised by even the most heinous truth and facts. But even the slightest lie, whomever it comes from, will make me short-tempered. I have to commend the Tribunal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we are entering an area where we should not be in.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. I will not praise the Tribunal. I did say ugly things about it. But had I not come here, I would have been in heaven a long time ago. So I'd like to thank everyone, from the cleaning lady to all the medical staff in the Bronovo Hospital for having saved my life. Thank you. I will continue co-operating. I regularly take medication, but half of my body is not functional and how functional the other part of my body is is something that you've explained. So thank you for your honest and humane testimony about my health. You are a friend of mine and a family member. Thank you to all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mladic. I take it that Dr. Falke highly appreciates your words.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that Dr. Falke confirms that. Dr. Falke, I'd like to thank you very much for coming to this courtroom and having answered the many questions we had for you. You may be -- you are excused and I would like to invite the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. FALKE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for your invitation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, we have 15 minutes left until the next break. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom? But since the usher is not there --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I need to have Mr. Nicholls come down. Your Honour, the Prosecution would be prepared to make oral submissions with respect to this now, if that would be a useful way to use the time. I don't know if Mr. Lukic feels prepared to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On what exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You said that you were going to invite medical -- submissions on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you give us some time that we most likely will invite you, but we would first like to see whether we give you any guidance on what we are mainly interested in and whether that should be oral submissions or written submissions, we'd still like to consider first.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, I anticipate Mr. Nicholls was watching the monitor and was on his way down. So if we can just give him a minute or two to arrive. [The witness takes the stand].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Welcome back in court, Mr. Nikolic. I'd like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Ms. Lindsay, I can't say that I'm very optimistic about concluding today. I think you even eye-witnessed the reasons for that so I'm not going to further explain to you. We will wait for Mr. Nicholls if he arrives in a minute and then, Mr. Petrusic, you're invited to continue your cross-examination. Mr. Groome, is your expectation of two minutes, is that experience-based or is it evidence --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls was watching the television. I trust Mr. Petrusic maybe not to go into anything too much controversy in the next few minutes and I would invite him to proceed and I'll handle any objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we could start and I think as a matter of fact our discussion allowed him to come down to this lower level. Mr. Petrusic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nikolic, yesterday we left off addressing the issue of humanitarian and other convoys. Let's stay with that topic for a while still.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to call up 65 ter 05568.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is Exhibit P1419.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, what you see on the screen is a document by the Main Staff of the VRS. If we look at its last page, we will see that the document is signed by Radivoje Miletic and that the date is the 15th of June, 1995. The document relates to the passage of an UNPROFOR convoy through -- into the enclaves and including Zepa -- or, I'm sorry, Srebrenica. Are you aware that the humanitarian aid was intended for the civilian population in the enclaves only?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You will therefore agree that military units, whatever the side they were on, could not get any supplies from these humanitarian shipments?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether they were able to or not is something that I don't know. They were supposed to if it was intended for the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the last page of both versions, where it reads: "Pay attention to fuel tanks for which we have the necessary tool (rod) ready to check the level of fuel in the tanks ...," and then there is an illegible part. "Carry out checks and allow movement along the mentioned routes." Mr. Nikolic, do you know why the levels of fuel contained in the tanks of the vehicles belonging to UNPROFOR were checked?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that I do know the reason. Specifically, when there were large convoys, and I mean the number of lorries --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, I'm going to stop you here. We heard evidence about this. If there's anything different, then put a focused question to the witness which deviates from the evidence we heard until now, but we should not hear again the same explanation. That's repetitious evidence the Chamber is not assisted by, and I don't remember that there was any dispute about - but I'm looking at the Prosecution - about the explanation given for the check on fuel levels that would be to take fuel out and then ... Let's proceed at this moment. I have a clear recollection so have my colleagues about having heard evidence on that. Therefore, any deviation, fine; no repetition.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, on page 1 of this document - can we have it shown on the screen, please - is this your signature, or rather, is this your handwriting, the one we see in the note?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything written at the top, including the numbers and the letters NOBP underlined do not reflect my handwriting. My handwriting is in the note below, "security officers shall witness detailed checks Nikolic M.," and this is my handwriting. I wrote it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you do the same in all the situations or in isolated cases?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not standard practice, i.e., that we should have a security organ or someone from security present at the check-point or any of the senior or commanding officers. But in this critical period, orders were given that there should be someone in addition to the team that was present at the Yellow Bridge at all times and they were -- would normally be people from security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And do you know the reasons behind this?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reasons are simple. Heightened checks of everything that was going into the enclave in this period of time, and I believe that you and of course I in particular was aware that preparations were underway for the take-over of the enclave, for offensive combat activities in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: At the time - and that's the 15th of July - the 15th of June --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: -- were you aware of impending combat activities?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, as an intelligence officer I didn't need to have it all spelled out. If you take just one situation, and that's the 30th and the 31st of May, and the activities that were underway on the 30th and 31st of May up until the 5th of June, all -- the combat activities undertaken by our forces in the area of Zeleni Jadar point to the fact that there would certainly follow combat activities from that particular direction. Let me be quite clear. Nobody told me in so many words that an operation was going to take place against Srebrenica on such and such a date, but all these were indications to me that preparations were underway for such an action on Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can we conclude that after the 5th of June you didn't have any intelligence to the effect that the Drina Corps units would launch an action against Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about official information from some of the officers of the Drina Corps, then it was some 15 to 20 days ahead of the operation itself that I received direct information that an operation on Srebrenica was being readied.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the sources of official information were? Were they oral or written?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, the official source of information was the Drina Corps command and that's -- that was General Zivanovic who visited the Bratunac Brigade. He was sitting together with me, Major Trisic, and some other officers from the brigade command. He was pointing to some sort of map and explaining to us that a plan of an attack against the enclave of Srebrenica was being put together.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, the map that General Zivanovic was showing to you, did it involve the burnt villages around Srebrenica and Bratunac in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't look into the map in detail. He was talking about an operational map that he had with him in the context of this attack against Srebrenica, and then he went on to explain what was being planned. So I wouldn't be able to comment on what was General's operational map.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted into evidence? Oh, yes, I'm sorry, it's already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm sorry to interrupt. No objection, but I'm noticing that the questions are coming before the interpretation is finished and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Again, I'm sorry to interrupt, but I'm just concerned that the transcript be complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, I notice that you also do not always take a short pause. Could you please keep that in mind, and Mr. Nikolic, you as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you. I'd like to call up document 65 ter 19393. In the Serbian version, the B/C/S version, it's page 2, starting with paragraph 1. And in English it's also page 1, paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, in paragraph 1 you say -- I apologise. I withdraw the question. If we look at the last page, can we agree that this is indeed your statement and that this is your signature? Can we have the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go back to page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, did you give the statement to the Trial Chamber in the Popovic case shortly before your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 1 of the statement you say: "The intentions or the first intention was to physically separate two enclaves, namely Zepa and Srebrenica; to liberate the Zeleni Jadar-Jasenovo-Milici road and in phase two to reduce the Srebrenica enclave to the town area." Do you stand by this position today?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I stand by everything I wrote in this statement including this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I'd like us to look at document --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or rather, can this document be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar -- Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. I would just say that if this document is to be admitted, for it to make sense one would also need to admit the document that it is a supplement to. As you see, this is a supplementary statement, and the paragraph just read out, paragraph 1 of the statement, is supplementing paragraph 1 of Mr. Nikolic's statement of facts and responsibilities. So just a quick background, Mr. Nikolic was called by the Trial Chamber in the Popovic case as a witness, and they used his statement of facts of responsibility from the time of his plea and they requested that he create the supplementary statement in order to clarify any issues in his initial statement. So sorry, that's a long objection -- answer. But I think both of them need to be in together for it to be comprehensible because what is sought to be admitted are corrections, additions, and clarifications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Isn't that in -- already in evidence? If you can give us the document number?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge. It's 65 ter 19394.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My intention was precisely to have the other statement admitted as well as the statement of facts made by Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So everything would be -- that means statement of facts, the statement to which this document we have now on the screen is a correction, and then this document. We don't have the numbers for all three yet I think -- yes, yes, of course. The statement of facts is already in evidence, but then the statement underlying this one -- yes, that's 19393 and 19394. Is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if this is the time for our break? I've lost track of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is time for our break, it certainly is. But, Madam Registrar, could we already assign numbers to the two documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Document 19393 receives number D300 and document 19394 receives number D301, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D300 and D301 are admitted into evidence. We'll take a break. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes and we'll resume at -- after the witness has left the courtroom, we'll resume at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I use the opportunity to invite the parties to make written submissions if they wish to do so on the -- on any matter discussed with Dr. Falke by the end of this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest, Mr. Petrusic, that exceptionally that we would continue until quarter past 2.00 now, that's five-quarters of an hour. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Could we have document P301 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you say P or D?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: If we look at the last page of this document, Mr. Nikolic, do you recognise your signature there?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the last page please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: That statement of facts and acceptance of responsibility dated 6th May. Mr. Nikolic, in paragraph 1 -- actually, the second paragraph, you said that during the attack of the take-over of the Srebrenica enclave by VRS forces and its occupation by the VRS forces in July of 1995, it was to cause the forcible removal of the entire Muslim population from Srebrenica to Muslim-held territory. You gave this statement under oath.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So when you changed a part of the agreement which related to your participation in Kravica and which related to the photograph, you had the opportunity to change some other parts?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time I wasn't thinking about that. I didn't analyse everything that was written down in detail. At the moment I analysed things, I consulted certain rules, certain instructions, and everything that relates to Srebrenica I tried to explain in the simplest of terms and to say very precisely what the goal was, what the intention was, what the military goal was, that was my intention. And to separate from the military goal the consequences that occurred after the fall of the enclave. That was my intention. And as for that, I didn't step away from what I said originally nor is there any particular difference between what I said and accepted before. This is just more detailed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You'll agree with me, Mr. Nikolic, that between this statement, the one that I quoted, and your statement given before the Trial Chamber in the Popovic case in document D300, which you had an opportunity to see, as far as the Defence is concerned there is a significant difference exactly when it comes to the intention because in document D300 you said that the intention was the physical separation of the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, while in your agreement and acceptance of responsibility when you talk of intention you do not talk about the physical separation of Srebrenica and Zepa. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please put to the witness what it reads. The one being the intentions of the VRS forces to cause the forcible removal of the entire Muslim population from Srebrenica, that was paragraph 1 of the statement. And then apparently now it reads: The first intention of the VRS was to physically separate two enclaves, the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica, to liberate the Zeleni Jadar-Jasenovo-Milici road and in phase two to reduce the Srebrenica enclave to the town area. The forcible removal of the entire Muslim population from Srebrenica was the result of the fall of the enclave and subsequent decisions. That is what we are talking about. I don't think that when you previously read a portion of the new statement to the witness, I think you did not read the second part of what he said. So please focus your questions not starting with where the difference is in the view of the Defence, but to find out whether the witness intended, as he just said, did not want to change his statement in essence or whether he just wanted to give further details. That is the issue and that is fair to the witness. Mr. Nikolic, did you have any intention by the second portion I read to you to change your initial statement about the intentions to cause the forcible removal of the entire Muslim population from Srebrenica? Or did you want to add something to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this additional statement I merely wanted to the extent possible to say what the first intention was of the VRS, what the following task was of the VRS, and what this entire operation grew into, so to speak. And of course I wanted to say that the decision on the entire forcible transfer of the population was made after the fall of Srebrenica. Srebrenica was lost and defeated militarily, and the VRS did not stop after it reached its first and second intention. It separated Srebrenica from the enclave, and as a result of the fall of the enclave we had the forcible transfer of the entire population and an empty enclave after the operation. That was my intention. I don't know whether I managed to explain clearly, but that was my intention to explain it so that it would be both clear to me and to others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you one additional question. What finally happened was the intended result although, if I understand you well, may not have been the intention right from the beginning but at least was the result intended at least after the fall of -- the military take-over of Srebrenica. Is that how we have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not exactly, not in its entirety. If we look at the document that we were discussing yesterday, that report and some other documents, there was talk in that about emptying Srebrenica enclave, and that was the real intention. But I wanted to show that was achieved militarily without respect for their own military decision which was to separate physically and that is not in dispute that the intention was a physical separation. And the next task was to create an enclave that would include the urban territory. However, even the military goal was overstepped and with the previous intention that was proclaimed as the political goal there followed a military defeat and the forcible transfer of the entire population. That was the goal. I was not able to explain everything in such detail in this statement. I wrote what I wrote and then I tried to explain everything during my testimonies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, you will agree with me that at that time, in July of 1995, the intention of the VRS -- as for the intention of the VRS, you did not have all the documents that you are referring to now and which you were able to inspect here during your trial?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll be completely honest. The entire time, from the time the enclave was set up, the entire time everything that was being done and everything that was done to the enclave led to a single goal which was for the enclave to disappear as an enclave and for it to be emptied and for it to become a Serbian territory. That was the declared goal the entire time. I can agree with you that this does not exist in writing in documents from that period, but that was the goal that was always declared and that was the permanent task. The task was to create conditions to empty the enclave. And if you're asking me whether I saw -- after I was arrested and after I saw the documents, if you're asking me whether certain documents show that intention to empty the enclave, I can answer that question because there are documents that show the exact intentions towards the Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, if that was a permanent intention, if I understand you correctly, from the time the enclaves were set up until their fall can you find a rational explanation for why that was not done earlier? Why were the enclaves not taken over before?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you about the Srebrenica enclave. I can give you at least ten reasons why it wasn't taken earlier. If you want me to and if the Court is interested in that, I will be happy to discuss this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, a brief explanation would not harm, although that's -- but primarily based on facts rather than if you could -- well, perhaps not all ten but if you have so many then at least in short lines give a few reasons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I worked in the intelligence department and I can explain it to you from that aspect and based on what I know for fact in that area. I can't talk about the other aspects. The first thing, first reason why Srebrenica wasn't occupied earlier or why not sufficient forces were engaged to occupy it was that in its surroundings the units that were around it were simply not prepared to attack Srebrenica, that's number one. Number two, the Skelani Battalion, my Bratunac Brigade, and the Milici Brigade -- as for the first two, I can claim with responsibility that they did not have the desire to attack Srebrenica because of all the circumstances and all the misfortune that they had gone through, both the Skelani and the Bratunac people. The next thing because the 28th Division was dispatched to Srebrenica and it was stronger than the forces that were surrounding the town, the 28th Division with its units, brigades, was militarily stronger than the Bratunac Brigade, the Skelani Battalion, and the Milici Brigade. There is no dispute. Also, at the very beginning we had high respect for the international forces that were intended for protection and nothing, I mean -- we didn't -- did not want to do anything to disrupt the relationships between UNPROFOR and the Serbian forces. And one more thing. When it comes to engagement and the attack on Srebrenica, the Bratunac Brigade was apart from this engaged at other fronts, among others in Pjenovac. Later after Srebrenica fell it was engaged in Trnovo. But they were engaged in Pjenovac and in other parts of the front. And finally to conclude, the basic conditions were not there to plan, organise, attack, and occupy Srebrenica. And just for the Trial Chamber and for you, we tried several times to enter the enclave - you can check that. In the 1st Infantry Battalion zone of responsibility, in the 3rd Infantry Battalion towards Crni Guber from Pribicevac and every time we suffered losses, we didn't do anything, and we had to withdraw. We suffered losses, we lost men, we failed to improve our tactical positions, and we got into a dispute with UNPROFOR with the international military forces that were protecting the enclave. So that was the reason why we never either entered it nor gathered sufficient forces to occupy Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: One more question in relation to this subject. You will agree with me that in 1993 after the establishment of the safe areas, the then-8th Operations Group in Srebrenica, later the 28th Division, was less well armed and had fewer soldiers than in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You might have got things mixed up but I'll help you. The 28th Division included units in the Srebrenica and Bratunac areas. The operations group is a higher level of organisation than the division. Those were the units that were in the 28th Division, and the members of the armed forces of Zepa. And of course including all those forces that existed before the fall of Cerska, Konjevic Polje, et cetera. So I don't agree with you that the 8th Operations Group was weaker in terms of combat than the 28th Division. As a group, it was composed of the units that I mentioned, the armed forces of Zepa, Srebrenica, Cerska, Konjevic Polje, Bratunac, and so on. So the 8th Operations Group was formed from these units and it was stronger both in terms of weapons and equipment and it had more men than the 28th Division when it was formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, whatever the name of the unit was that was stationed in Srebrenica, after the establishment of the safe areas in May of 1993, it was -- it had fewer weapons and had fewer soldiers than it did in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can agree with that statement. The enclave was established on the 18th of July and not May, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, you're talking about the forcible transfer of the entire Muslim population. Are you aware of cases from those areas when the war started in the area of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina that in places where the army was defeated, the army of either side, the civilian population would also withdraw behind the army?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would put it the other way around. The civilian population would withdraw ahead of the army not behind the army. The civilians would be leaving those axes or territories where combat was being executed, and this is correct. The civilians would leave before the soldiers would arrive or attain a certain line. So I'm just being a little more precise, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, in paragraph 6 of your statement of facts somewhere in the middle of that paragraph you talked about the units that were present in Potocari on the 12th of July and you also talked about that here. Could you please tell me how you identified the Drina Corps military police units? And just permit me to finish my question. How large was that unit? What was its strength, that unit in Potocari, that was under the command of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military police of the Drina Corps was frequently engaged with me in Bratunac frequently. I know that this police unit and people from the 65th Protection Regiment, I know them by face, I know what they look like. And I know for a fact that members of the military police, the corps military police, were in Bratunac on the 13th in the sector of Potocari. I cannot say -- I cannot say under whose command they were at that time in Potocari, who had brought them, I cannot tell you that. And I cannot tell you the number of the policemen that were engaged. I don't know the strength of any of the units that I referred to, but I know the people personally from certain units that I refer to. So there is no doubt that they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So are you able to say if they came in an organised manner, as a unit, with a command of their own?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that's a question for me. I believe that all the units that were there, I think that now as well, that all the units that were there on whatever grounds arrived in a planned and organised manner. But to be precise, I am not ruling out that certain groups came on their own initiative and so on. Things like that happen in any operation and after an operation. So I'm not ruling it out, but for the serious units, the police forces, I really don't know. My military police never went anywhere without going pursuant to an order of the commander or the deputy commander. That is my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So now we're talking about the presence of these units in Potocari. Would you agree with me that somebody had to have been in command of all those units? Do you know who it was who in command of those units in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command of all the units?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The command of all the units who were in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that at the very beginning all the units that were engaged in the Krivaja operation, the Srebrenica operation, in the beginning were under the command of the Drina Corps Chief of Staff, General Krstic, and then when they arrived - this is information that reached me, this is what I found out - once General Mladic arrived, he was the main commander of the operation, the Commander-in-Chief of the operation. This is what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that in the period that you are talking about up until the 11th of July --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you asked me specifically about who was in command of the units who were in the Krivaja operation. If I understood you correctly. So as for the combat part I know for a fact, this is what was conveyed to me, this is what was conveyed to all of us, that with the arrival of General Ratko Mladic he took over the control and command of all the units that were executing the combat actions. And I assume and according to military logic, all the engaged military units right until the end of the operation were under the command of the commander, the most senior officer who happened to be in the area of responsibility. This is military logic. I don't know if it was really like that or not is something that I cannot say, I cannot analyse that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The military units that were pursuant to the order engaged in the attack on Srebrenica completed their military tasks - if I can refer to it on that way - on the 11th of July in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: My main question, my initial question was on the 12th and the 13th of July in Potocari, all these elements, all the units that were concentrated there, and these are units of the MUP and special police units and the units that you talked about, who was commanding their units in the UN base? Who was in command of those units?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, those units were not in the base. They were there where the people were, where the civilians were. On the 12th, based on what I know, the units engaged in the operation was under the direct command of their commanders, the commanders of the units engaged in the Potocari actions were commanding their units. The special MUP brigade was in command of Ljubisa Borovcanin directly through his senior officers who were engaged in Potocari; Dusko Jevic and the units that were engaged there. The units that were from the Bratunac Brigade were under the responsibility of Vidoje Blagojevic, their commander. As for the forces engaged from the Drina Corps command, they were under the responsibility of the commander who was engaged there as well as the senior officers from the Drina Corps command, like Vujadin Popovic, who is a professional organ commanding the special forces, the military police, and Kosoric who was also there. As for the Bratunac Brigade elements, Vidoje Blagojevic was responsible for the execution of that assignment. And myself, I was the person responsible for the execution of tasks ordered for the forces that were under my command. I think that as for the units from the 65th Protection Regiment, the senior officers were in command of them, the officers who brought them there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Really, I apologise. Parts of the 10th Sabotage Unit were under the responsibility of the Main Staff and that was Colonel Radislav Jankovic because he was from the intelligence administration, and the reconnaissance units were directly under the intelligence organ and the Chief of Staff. This is what I know in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And the units that were on the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road going towards Konjevic Polje, did they maintain their independent commands there as well?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you know and I'm saying this for the Trial Chamber, you know what I'm going to say, and that is that police forces were always up until the beginning of the war -- I can conditionally say in some kind of covert conflict concerning the command and control of those units. What I know for a fact is that they always had command and control over their own units when they would be carrying out joint tasks with the army. They did, it's true, report in and they would come to the area of responsibility - and I know this for a fact as well - they would seek to find out what their tasks were within an operation and then they would almost for the most part organised their own reconnaissance, preparations for the operation, and everything else. And then of course when they carried out all of that, then in agreement with whoever was in charge of the operation they would carry out that operation in -- jointly, jointly, and carry out their joint tasks together in the same area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And could the same conclusion be drawn for the 13th of July according to what you know? And in relation to the participation of the special forces of the police of the MUP of Republika Srpska? Would your conclusion be the same?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My conclusion is that the task given to the civilian police after the combat part of the operation ended on the 11th and the transfer to the Kravica-Sandici-Pervani-Konjevic Polje road was actually a police task, securing the road was a police task and that is how I view that. In view of the fact that I know who from the police forces was in Bratunac, I'm thinking of the policemen and the senior officers, I can tell you with a great degree of certainty that the police forces were subordinated to their chief of centre. And in the area of engagement in that conditionally speaking combat assignment, all the units were subordinated to the commander of the MUP special brigade, who in this case was Ljubisa Borovcanin. So all the engaged forces on the Kravica-Sandici-Lolici-Konjevic Polje road were under the command of Ljubisa Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrusic, I'm trying to understand questions and answers. Mr. Nikolic, when you talk about the police forces, having their own command, was the situation -- there should be no loud speaking - you talk about the army, VRS, and you are talking about the police forces. Now, are there any facts to your knowledge which would either demonstrate that the police forces were acting independently from what the operational purposes were from the army or that they were acting in accordance with what the VRS highest command had as its plans, its operational plans?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps I was a bit too detailed. It is absolutely the way you say and I think you understood perfectly what I said, and that is that they acted within one operation together at the same tasks. So I'm just talking about one segment, the segment of the immediate command of those units because commanders insisted, commanders of the units, insisted that they should not be placed under the command of a superior who should issue direct orders to them. Let's say, for example, Ljubisa Borovcanin went and he was the superior who agreed on all the activities as part of the operation, the military operation, but later they insisted that they should be commanders, that they do separate reconnaissance, that they plan it there, but it was all as part of the operation and joint action. So in military terminology, that co-operation, the agreement, the engagement on a common task assignment is called joint action, joint action on the same assignment of two different structures which are participating in an operation and have the same objective. I don't know if I am a bit more clear now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's clear to me. One next question, the police forces and the army, do you have any knowledge on how they agreed on this joint operation, was it the commanders discussing the matter with each other? Was there any competition between the VRS command and the police command? Do you have any knowledge about that? If not, tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I know is that the engagement of those forces, the MUP combat units - and this was the special brigade of the MUP - this was something that was discussed at the highest level, the minister of the interior, at that level and at the level of the army. This was an agreement on the engagement at that level. What I know is that they never -- of course, they received certain separate assignments outside of the army, but these were all military assignments as far as I know. Both structures talk about the special MUP brigade and the military, and so both of those forces always would receive their assignments from the top level, from their superior officers, commands, staffs, and then they would realise or implement those tasks in the field jointly. Yes, there was small conflicts, minor disagreements between the MUP and the MUP forces, and they were allegedly -- Karadzic's forces, the president's forces. And the army was again more inclined towards General Mladic. So along that line there was a conflict which went on for a while. This is what I know, although I'm not really familiar with that top level sufficiently. I don't have any comments on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll not ask you any further questions on factual matters at that level. Please proceed, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, do you have any knowledge about the 13th of July, about who issued the order to the MUP special brigade to deploy along the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is that Borovcanin, they issued -- they were given the order to deploy along that road by Borovcanin and chief of centre Dragomir Vasic, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And do you know if Vasic or Borovcanin, that police structure, took the decision to take these Muslim soldiers prisoner, or rather, the Muslims who happened to be in the area?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of such a decision. I don't believe I ever saw such a decision, that they had been given orders to take prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Let's take it this way. If Muslims gathered in large numbers in the territory of Sandici, was that a territory under the control of the MUP forces?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In that period of time, was Kravica also under the control of the MUP forces?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We could say yes when it comes to Kravica. There was only one squad deployed, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Who could have taken that decision to have the Muslims transferred from Sandici to Kravica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a logical answer to that question, but I don't want to manipulate it. The decisions or the decision could have and should have been taken by the most senior commanding officer in the field. So the logical answer would be that it would be Ljubisa Borovcanin who would have taken that decision, he was personally engaged there, or Dragomir Vasic who had his headquarters in the Bratunac public security station and his police forces were engaged in that area. But I have never seen a document to that effect. If you do, perhaps I forgot about it, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: According to what you were able to learn at the time and later, killings occurred in the Kravica farm co-operative. Can you tell us who the perpetrators were?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can tell you is that after the crime took place I received an order from the Drina Corps command to inquire into two or three -- to three things and that was which structure had committed the crime and the other question in focus was whether army troops participated in it, including members of the Bratunac Brigade. I went out in the field and established that it had been perpetrated by the police forces. I was not interested in which particular structure at the time or in the meantime. I established that it had been done by the police and that there was no participation of the army in it, that nobody had ordered any soldiers to participate in it; however, that there were two or three soldiers from my brigade who under no one's orders happened to be there. They were simply Kravica inhabitants who - and I will say this although it's ugly - to take revenge, who wanted to take revenge. One of these had had his father killed in prison and the other had had his brother and the third had been wounded seriously by Muslims. I informed the command of the corps that the crime in Kravica had been committed by police, that there was no organised or planned engaged of the army, and that when murder was committed, two or three soldiers from the 1st Infantry Battalion of my brigade were present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, a moment, please. Can we move on to paragraph 10 of your statement. It's page 5 in both versions, paragraph 10. We have the proper page in English, it's page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. I have a different version, where the numeration is different, but in Serbian it's page 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You see it on your screen now, is that a copy you have you're working from?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In the middle of the last paragraph, Mr. Nikolic, we can read as follows: "At the meeting there was open discussion of the murder operation and all the participants indicated that they had been reporting to their various chains of command."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where are you reading, Mr. -- where are you reading?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm reading from the middle of the last paragraph of item 10 on page.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The killing operation was openly discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, no speaking aloud. I have to repeat it again and again. If you would like to consult with counsel, then, Mr. Lukic or Mr. Stojanovic, you do it silently. Well, if you want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I consult?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so but only if your voice remains at inaudible levels. That's not inaudible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, would you take care that Mr. Mladic lowers his voice. Mr. Lukic, this was the last consultation. Mr. Mladic was not -- apparently not willing to lower his voice. So for the next 25 minutes, no further consultations. Please proceed, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, do you have information about how the reporting was carried out? Was it by telegram? Over the phone? Or through some other means?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When this particular phrasing is concerned, this sentence that you've just read out, I kindly ask you to jointly view the sentence you've just read out with what I said in the supplementary statement. It literally said what this paragraph applied to. Let's look at the supplementary statement, please, because there to avoid any misunderstanding we will see what it was that I corrected and said that this was what actually happened in quite precise terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, after signing the statement on the 6th of May, 2003, on the 28th, the 29th, and the 30th of May, and the 12th of June, 2003, you were interviewed by the Prosecution, you spoke to them. Was that the time when you made these corrections?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You will have the exact date when I made these corrections and submitted them to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Without going into any discussion about it, you submitted this to the Chamber on the 16th of April, 2009; is that right? Now, what I'm asking you is this: After the agreement you reached with the Prosecution on the 6th of May, 2003, you had occasion to speak to the Prosecution and you did speak to them over the course of four or five days. At the time during these discussions which were supposed to provide a clarification of the agreement, did you make the corrections that you are referring to today?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Before submitting these corrections to the Trial Chamber on the 16th of April, 2009, did you refuse to appear as a Prosecution witness in the Popovic case in 2007?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true. I did not refuse to appear as a witness for the Prosecution. I simply insisted that my first statement of facts have certain clarifications and corrections made which I thought were important. They were simply out of my remit of work and were not written in precise terms and were thus liable to different interpretations. I asked that these issues be defined quite in precise terms in a statement that I asked be drawn up. And one more thing, I want to explain one other thing. To be frank, I wasn't even aware of the various formulations, I didn't pay particular attention to that. There are certain parts which relate to control, co-ordination, and my lawyers were reassuring me that this was of no significance, that the Chamber knew that I was not charged with command responsibility but rather individual responsibility and that I should not be any attention to that. Now, by the time I realised that this was very important, I sat down, took a pen and paper, and wrote down the sequence of events as they happened and as I thought should be reflected in the statement that I wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, you have no military training --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: You have military training.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: -- and you did graduate from university course which gave you specialist knowledge. In that context, your assertion that you had no competence in certain areas is not something that I can accept and I apologise to Their Honours for making this comment. My basic question was this: After meeting with the Prosecution on the 19th of October, 2007, did you accept their call to appear as a witness in the Popovic case before making these corrections?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never refused to testify in any of the instances when the Prosecution called me, never. So we didn't agree on the issues that we are now discussing and that much is true, we didn't agree. I claimed something else and I asked that a different statement be made. It's not going to be the end of the world if I made a mistake, but perhaps I didn't meet up with understanding or willingness on their part. Still, I would never have refused to appear as a witness regardless of whether these corrections made or not. Had the Prosecution called me, had the Trial Chamber issued me with a summons, I would have appeared here just as I did when the Trial Chamber called me as their own witness. I would have no reason to refuse and this is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So you are telling us that in October 2007 the Prosecution did not tell you at all that you should appear as a witness in the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That is a total misstatement of what the witness just said is being put to him as what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, this objection is sustained. Would you please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, did you ask at this point in time that you be issued with a summons from the Chamber so that you may appear as witness?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, where would I get the authority that will allow me to ask for the Chamber to issue me with anything? I honoured every order given by a Trial Chamber in any trial. At one point in time after speaking with the Prosecution, I was told that the Prosecution gave up on the idea of having me appear as a witness in that trial and I respected that decision. I don't know the dates. But after a certain period of time, the Trial Chamber in that case informed me that I would have to appear as a witness of the Chamber in that case. When I received word that I should come and appear here, I did come and testify for some six or seven days.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you respond to that summons? Did you testify and did you respond to the summons issued by the court of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo in all cases?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell what that case was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Petrusic. The witness has just answered "I don't think so." Now, your question was -- relates to two different things. I'm not sure what he's answering to as a result. You're saying did you respond to that summons, you are talking about the summons here, and then you continue to say: "Did you testify and did you respond to the summons issued by the court of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo in all cases?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These are two questions it seems to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, that's what I'm saying. There are two questions here. Now what shall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Shall we start with the first one, then? Perhaps that -- did you respond to the summons issued to you to appear before the -- this court, Mr. Nikolic, in the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you respond to summonses issued to you to appear before the court of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in two cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you refuse in other cases to appear upon being summoned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not explicitly, but I responded to their request and I told them why I shouldn't testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you talked about the reporting and you said that everybody reported to their superior. Along your line of intelligence, who was Beara's superior?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you misinterpreted once again what I said yesterday. In my testimony yesterday I said that those who were present at the meeting referred -- referred to the orders by their superiors when it comes to prisoners and when it comes to the destiny of the prisoners, that's what I said. And as for the second part, I can answer you now. As far as I know, the immediate superior in the intelligence sector of the Main Staff, Beara's superior was General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Let's move on, Mr. Nikolic. After that meeting, we are still on paragraph 10, you went to your command?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And you informed Colonel Blagojevic about what happened at that meeting. Could you tell us in a little more detail how Colonel Blagojevic reacted? Did he know about all of that? Did he have some information from elsewhere? Or did he have any other knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I testified about this several times and including Colonel Blagojevic's reactions. My conclusions both then and now were that Blagojevic knew what was happening in Bratunac on the 13th, including the 12th and the 13th. And since you're asking me, he wasn't surprised at all. You must also accept that the brigade commander in whose zone of responsibility actions were under way, combat operations, and other actions which you are talking about, he would have had to know more than me because my commander was a colonel, he was a professional, he was the brigade commander. And surely he had more information and more contacts based on the line of command than I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did he know about the decision regarding the killings?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My impression was that he knew about all of that, he knew about what was happening. Among others, he knew about that intention too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The first killings that happened were on the 13th of July in Kravica. Do you know how these killings came to happen?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you what I heard, what I heard like everybody else. What I heard from people who were in the police units -- of course after everything had happened and after the war ended even, was that there was an incident and that was the reason for killing those people en masse. There was an incident in which one policeman was killed, one was wounded. As far as I know, it had to do with taking somebody's rifle. And after that incident, they killed everybody they found there. That is what I know, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So those killings happened without any control or any order; is that your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can draw conclusions like you can, but I don't know for a fact how these killings happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Let's assume that that's how it was; namely, we still don't have any formulated order, whether it's oral or in writing, or any other kind of order regarding the treatment of those people who were in Bratunac that night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. It says: "Let's assume that's how it was," which I think is referring to his previous question and answer where Mr. Nikolic said he didn't know and didn't want to speculate about whether there was an order. And then he continues: "... we still don't have any formulated order, whether it's oral or in writing..." I don't know if that's also meant to be a hypothetical. I'm sorry, but it doesn't -- I don't think it's fair to ask about a hypothetical and then say, well, if we accept this hypothetical, then there is no order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, you are invited to reformulate your question, and questions usually are not of great assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, do you know anything about any kind of an order from the time that the killings happened in Kravica in the afternoon to your meeting with Colonel Beara around midnight between the 13th or the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, one of the previous answers ended with that is what I know, nothing more. You're asking for the "more" of which the witness said he didn't know. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When you told Colonel Blagojevic, was anyone else in the office with you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've already testified about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Everything that happened in Potocari on the 12th of July, did you also inform Colonel Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I informed Colonel Blagojevic about everything that was happening in those days in the Bratunac Brigade zone of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Were those meetings always between just the two of you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that detail. I don't know whether I was always alone when I talked to him. I'm talking about official reporting to Colonel Blagojevic and I am not sure whether we were always alone, but on a few occasions we were alone in his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: On the 13th, before and after this meeting, do you know where Colonel Jankovic, Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic, and Kosoric were?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 12th and the 13th?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: No. My question was whether from what happened in Kravica to your meeting with Colonel Beara, so whether you knew where Colonel Jankovic, Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic, and Lieutenant-Colonel Kosoric were, I believe he was a lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, you're making it very difficult for all of us to understand your question. How do you link the whereabouts of these people with from what happened in Kravica? I don't understand the question and I don't know whether anybody can be able to answer this question. If you want to know where these people were at that time, just tell the time -- let the witness say whether he knew where they were during that time, but not to say from where what happened. I'm not quite sure what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, do you know where these three men were between 4.30 on the 13th of July to midnight on the same day?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, I'm looking at the clock. We have to adjourn in two minutes and I have a few matters to briefly address. Mr. Nikolic, we would like to see you back tomorrow morning. You already -- I hereby instruct you again that you should not speak or communicate in any other way about your testimony, whether given already or still to be given. You can follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, where are we in terms of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that I will finish during the first or the second session -- no, I'm sorry, one session is an hour, so I will probably need two sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll ask the Registrar further for timing. The problem is that you asked for a viva voce witness more time than the Prosecution asked, which is not within the usual guidance. And apart from that issue, you may have noticed the Chamber considered that you wasted some time here and there. So would you please be very focused and we'll further consider whether two sessions are available to you. Could you already give us an indication -- I know it's difficult, Mr. Nicholls, at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: My estimate would be about half an hour at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Half an hour. Yes. Then before we adjourn, I'm addressing you as well, Ms. Lindsay, because you had difficulties, I think, in staying with us for longer than today. Have you considered - of course you are counsel of the witness - have you considered how to resolve this matter?

utterances.speaker: MS. LINDSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have been speaking with the Registry. I will stay until Mr. Nikolic is finished with his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which will be tomorrow. That's -- your flexibility is highly appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MS. LINDSAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will adjourn for the day and we'll resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 5th of June, Courtroom I, 9.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 5th day of June, 2013, at 9.30 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
